summary: Return the values of all nodes exactly k edges away from a target node in a binary tree.
mainInsight: Distance can go up through the parent as well as down, so treat the tree as an undirected graph: record each node's parent (or build adjacency), then BFS from the target for k levels.
invariant: At the start of BFS level d, the queue holds exactly the nodes at distance d from the target.

approaches.name: Parent map + BFS from target
approaches.summary: DFS to record parents, then BFS over left, right and parent.

approaches.name: Adjacency list + BFS
approaches.summary: Build an undirected graph keyed by value, then BFS.

approaches.name: Single DFS with distances to target
approaches.summary: DFS returns distance to the target; collect nodes at k - d in the other subtree.

personalSolution.approach: Undirected adjacency list keyed by value + BFS from target
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. Keying by value works because values are unique; if k exceeds the tree height, BFS empties and you correctly return [].

commonMistakes: Only searching down from the target, missing nodes reached through the parent.
No visited set, so the BFS bounces between child and parent.
Not handling k larger than any distance (should return []).
edgeCases: k larger than the tree's diameter -> [].

promptVariants: Why is a DFS down from the target not enough?
What does searching only target's subtree miss?
options: Nodes reached through the target's parent
Nodes at depth exactly k in the whole tree
Leaves that are k levels below the target
Nothing, the subtree holds all answers
cards.answer: Nodes reached through the target's parent
cards.explanation: In example 1, node 1 is at distance 2 from target 5 via the root; it is not in 5's subtree.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Nodes at depth exactly k in the whole tr: Depth from the root is a different question.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Leaves that are k levels below the targe: Those are found by a downward search.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Nothing, the subtree holds all answers: Example 1 already includes node 1 outside the subtree.

promptVariants: Why does the BFS need a seen set even though a tree has no cycles?
What happens without the seen set?
options: Parent edges let BFS walk back up
Trees can have cycles through the root
The parent map might contain duplicate keys
It is needed only when values repeat
cards.answer: Parent edges let BFS walk back up
cards.explanation: Each edge can now be crossed in both directions; without seen, a node revisits its parent and itself, producing wrong levels.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The parent map might contain duplicate k: Each node has one parent entry.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It is needed only when values repeat: Values are unique; revisits come from undirected edges.

promptVariants: Node 1 is the left child of 0 and has children 3 and 2. Target 2, k = 1?
cards.explanation: Node 2 is a leaf, so its only neighbour is its parent 1.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[1, 3]: Only the parent is one edge away.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time of parent map + BFS.
cards.explanation: Building the parent map visits each node once, and BFS enqueues each node at most once.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n * k): Each node is enqueued once, not once per level.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(k): The parent pass alone reads all n nodes.

promptVariants: The parent map and seen set use O(___) space.

cards.explanation: One entry per node in each structure.
